articles.title: In 2008, Minnesota tested pervious concrete on a road with light traffic; long-term monitoring found ride quality held up, while vacuuming helped maintain drainage
articles.summary: Discover how Minnesota's 2008 trial of pervious concrete on low-volume roads proved effective for drainage, ride quality, and noise reduction in cold weather, emphasizing the importance of maintenance for successful implementation.
articles.body: When rain falls on a typical road or parking lot, it has relatively few options for where to go. Because standard concrete and asphalt protect the ground, water flows into storm drains that frequently empty into rivers untreated after sliding off the surface and picking up oil and grit along the way. To address that, pervious concrete was created. Rainfall flows directly through the surface and soaks into the soil below because it is filled with many tiny, linked spaces.The idea made sense in theory, but engineers in cold climates had concerns. A surface full of holes may break up if water freezes within, and salt, snow ploughs and passing traffic could permanently block up the pores. So, to find out, Minnesota erected test portions on a low-usage route in 2008. Monitoring at MnROAD found that ride quality remained adequate for roads with light traffic over the years. MnDOT's research summary reports that regular vacuum maintenance, more than twice a year, helped maintain the pavement's benefits, including drainage.The results are most relevant to village lanes, driveways and residential streets that carry light traffic in snowy climates. The MnROAD tests found that ride quality remained suitable for roads with light traffic, while regular maintenance helped protect drainage. Researchers also recorded differences in smoothness and permeability between the test cells, so the findings should not be treated as a guarantee that every pervious concrete surface will perform the same way.Why Minnesota did the trialTo appreciate why the trial mattered, it helps to understand what officials were seeking to learn. Pervious pavements had promise for crowded metropolitan areas where enormous quantities of contaminated runoff end up in drains, but no one knew how they would handle Minnesota’s harsh environment, how much maintenance they would require or what their effect would be on groundwater quality. We got an early glimpse with a pervious concrete driveway completed in 2005.In autumn 2008, the team extended the work by installing three test sections on MnROAD's Low Volume Road, a two lane research loop about 2.5 miles (about 4 km) long. The design and early performance of the sections are documented in MnDOT's 2011 final report.Two of the cells were full-depth pervious concrete, one constructed on sandy soil and one on clay. The third was a porous concrete overlay about 4 inches (10 centimetres) thick on an existing slab. The full-depth cells are 7 inches (approximately 18 cm) of pervious concrete atop 4 inches of railway ballast and 8 inches of crushed stone.The loop functions like a laboratory. A five-axle semi-trailer weighing 80,000 pounds (about 36 tonnes) repeatedly travels along the inner lane, while the outer lane remains exposed to the weather. Crews plough and salt the route much like they would any low-volume road. Thermocouples and moisture sensors embedded in the cells track the frequency of ground freeze and thaw, the movement of temperatures through the layers and the effectiveness of water drainage.What years of testing showedResearchers repeatedly measured ride quality, noise, friction, surface roughness, surface condition and permeability across seasons. During the first full year, friction readings taken with a smooth tyre ranged from 45 to 55, above the threshold of 25 that the report identified for corrective action.Noise readings on the pervious concrete cells ranged from 97 to 100.5 decibels, compared with about 103.5 decibels on a neighbouring concrete cell with transverse tining. The test results suggested that the porous surface absorbed more noise from the interaction between tyres and the road. Ride quality varied during the testing period. Reported roughness values ranged from 3.10 to 6.40 metres per kilometre, depending on the season, wheel path and measurement method. The report also noted that hand finishing during installation affected surface smoothness. Even so, MnDOT's longer-term analysis found that the test cells retained ride quality suitable for roads with light traffic.The cells did not behave identically. Researchers poured buckets of water onto the pavement and found that the wetting reached the full width of the inner lane but only about half the width of the outer lane. Separate density measurements suggested that the voids were unevenly distributed, with calculated porosity averaging from 13 to 19% in the cells. The report identified differences in construction and material inside the pores as possible explanations.Why vacuuming mattersGrit, leaves and winter sand can clog the connected pores, making maintenance important for drainage. In a demonstration about a year after construction, researchers used a vacuum truck with its brush switched off because mechanical brushing could push debris deeper into the gaps. The cells appeared relatively clean before the demonstration, and the drainage results changed only slightly after cleaning. The sandy subgrade cell continued to drain in 6 seconds, while the clay subgrade cell improved from 17 to 15.5 seconds.These results describe one demonstration and do not establish that regular maintenance is unnecessary or determine the ideal cleaning schedule. MnDOT's broader evaluation found that regular vacuuming more than twice a year helped maintain pervious pavement performance. Vacuuming and mechanical brushing are different procedures, so leaving the brush switched off during this test does not contradict the recommendation for recurring vacuum maintenance.The Minnesota trial does not establish that pervious concrete will work equally well on every road. It indicates that the material can be suitable for roads carrying light traffic in cold climates when installation is carefully controlled and drainage is maintained. The results also show why construction quality matters: differences in the distribution of pores and in surface smoothness affected the test cells. Anyone considering the material should account for local weather, traffic levels and the cost of regular vacuum maintenance.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.summary: In 2022, Florida buyer Nilesh Undavia put down $1.65 million for a luxury condominium that was supposed to be ready by the end of the year.
articles.body: In 2022, Florida buyer Nilesh Undavia put down $1.65 million for a luxury condominium that was supposed to be ready by the end of the year. Four years later, the apartment remains unfinished and his deposit has yet to be returned, even after an arbitration ruling in his favour. The case is part of a growing dispute surrounding Boca Raton’s Mandarin Oriental Residences, where buyers are seeking refunds as the developer faces a $417.7 million foreclosure lawsuit, according to reporting by The New York Times, The Real Deal and The Coastal Star. The development, part of the ambitious Via Mizner project in South Florida, was marketed as an upscale destination combining luxury residences, hotel services and resort-style amenities. Instead, years of construction delays, mounting debts and legal disputes have left prospective homeowners uncertain about when, or whether, they will receive the properties they paid for.A luxury project that missed its deadlinesPenn-Florida Companies unveiled plans for Via Mizner in 2015, proposing a 2.3-million-square-foot development featuring a Mandarin Oriental hotel, branded condominiums, rental apartments and high-end retail and dining spaces. The original completion target was late 2017. The wider development was designed to offer residents access to amenities including a swimming pool, golf facilities, a country club and a wine cellar. Buyers were also paying for the appeal of living in a property associated with the internationally recognised Mandarin Oriental luxury hospitality brand.However, the project has fallen substantially behind schedule. The rental apartments are operational, but the hotel and condominium components have encountered serious financial and construction problems. Penn-Florida has attributed the delays to a combination of the pandemic, hurricanes, rising construction costs, supply-chain disruptions and higher interest rates. The company has said that close to $1 billion has been invested in the wider development.Buyers fight to recover million-dollar depositsUndavia’s case illustrates the financial risks facing buyers who committed substantial sums to properties that have yet to be completed. He agreed to purchase a four-bedroom condominium for $5.5 million in 2022, paying a deposit of $1.65 million. The apartment was advertised with two terraces and distant ocean views, but the promised delivery date passed without the home being completed. Although Undavia secured an arbitration decision directing the developer to refund his deposit with interest, he has reportedly still not received the money.He is not alone. According to The Coastal Star and The Real Deal, 13 buyers have filed lawsuits against the condominium developer over missed completion deadlines. Deposits in several cases have ranged from approximately $1 million to $2 million. Other cases have produced different outcomes. One couple obtained a judgment of approximately $1.98 million, while another buyer dispute involving Undavia and his wife was settled for $2.1 million, according to the South Florida Business Journal. A separate lawsuit filed in October 2026 by another prospective buyer seeking the return of a $1.23 million deposit highlights how the dispute continues to affect purchasers.A $418 million foreclosure adds to the uncertaintyThe condominium tower is now at the centre of a major legal battle between Penn-Florida and its construction lenders. In July 2026, a lender group affiliated with Apollo Global Management filed a foreclosure lawsuit seeking approximately $417.7 million from the developer’s condominium-owning affiliate. The claim includes a $270 million loan principal, advances made toward project expenses, interest and other charges.The lenders allege that the developer defaulted on its loan obligations, missed repayment and construction deadlines, and failed to maintain the required hotel management agreement. Penn-Florida has challenged the lenders’ account. In a separate lawsuit seeking more than $500 million in damages, the developer alleges that the lenders interfered with construction decisions and withheld funding, contributing to the project’s difficulties. Those allegations remain disputed and have not been established as facts by a court. The adjoining hotel has also entered bankruptcy proceedings, adding another layer of uncertainty to the development.Could buyers lose their deposits?One of the biggest concerns for purchasers is whether they can recover money already released to the developer for construction. Florida law permits developers to use certain portions of condominium buyers’ deposits for construction when the relevant contractual conditions are met. Consequently, the amount a buyer can recover may depend on how the deposit was handled, the terms of the purchase agreement and the outcome of the legal proceedings.The foreclosure could complicate matters further because secured lenders generally have priority over many other creditors. Buyers whose deposits have already been spent may face a more difficult path to recovering their money than those whose funds remain protected in escrow. The dispute could also undermine the development’s luxury appeal. Mandarin Oriental issued a termination notice to Penn-Florida in 2025 over alleged contractual breaches, including unpaid expenses and reporting obligations. The developer maintains that its agreement with the brand remains in effect, leaving the residences’ branding uncertain.Penn-Florida has indicated that construction could resume and that some homes might be completed within nine months once work restarts. However, no clear restart date has been established. For buyers who invested millions in the promise of a finished luxury home, the immediate question is no longer simply when they can move in. articles.title: Serbia votes as students seek to unseat Aleksandar Vucic in snap election
articles.summary: BELGRADE — Serbia is voting on Sunday as a mass student protest movement seeks to unseat long-time populist ​leader Aleksandar Vucic in the biggest challenge to his rule for more than a decade.
articles.body: BELGRADE — Serbia is voting on Sunday as a mass student protest movement seeks to unseat long-time populist ​leader Aleksandar Vucic in the biggest challenge to his rule for more than a decade. The snap parliamentary elections, called by Vucic in ‌September, come after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against perceived corruption and creeping authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of 16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024. The students have since gained widespread support. Unusually long lines formed at polling stations in Belgrade and Novi Sad before the start of voting at 7 a.m.. Voting ​ends at 8 p.m. with first indications of results expected around two hours later. A student victory would be a profound political shift in ​the Balkan country of some 6 million people, reminiscent of the defeat of Hungary’s Viktor Orban in April. It also potentially ⁠offers a blueprint for other student movements across Europe, which have taken to the streets in recent weeks to protest, in some cases violently, against poor education standards and ​a lack of prospects. But Vucic, who resigned from his second term as president to run again for prime minister, is a strong incumbent. Many voters thank him ​for pulling Serbia from economic obscurity and orchestrating a period of sustained modernisation including new highways, railways, schools and hospitals. “I came out early today because the students called us,” said Ana, 30, at a polling station in Belgrade. Opinion polls predict tight race Domestically, Vucic has pledged higher pensions and public sector salaries, investment in state healthcare and subsidies for young couples. On ​the international stage, he has balanced closer ties with China, a major investor, and Russia, Serbia’s traditional ally and principal supplier of natural gas, while leaving ​the door open to joining the European Union. The students’ domestic agenda aims to root out graft and improve schooling, but they have been quieter on their international ambitions. Their list ‌of 250 ⁠largely unknown candidates includes university professors, actors and farmers, and is led by cardiologist Ilija Srdanovic. Opinion polls predict a tight race. In an Ipsos poll published on Thursday, Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) is seen leading with 47% of votes versus 40% for the students. But other polls have put the students in the lead. Student protests increase pressure The student-led street protests sparked by the station disaster quickly became the biggest in a generation, calling for Vucic to step down. Rights groups ​and activists say repression has worsened in ​the period since. Bogdan Pavkovic was one ⁠of thousands in central Belgrade for a final student rally on Thursday. He said he wants to change “this awful, horrendous system which cheats on us, which spies on us, which beats us.” Vucic’s office and the Interior Ministry did not respond to ​requests for comment. Vucic and the SNS have repeatedly denied accusations of repression, corruption and spying on their opponents. ​He says the students ⁠are funded by foreign agents in Croatia and Montenegro, a charge the students dismiss. “This has been one of the most difficult but the most emotional campaigns,” Vucic told his supporters on Thursday. “We stood against those who wanted to destroy Serbia.” Relations sour with E.U. Relations with the E.U. have frayed as the bloc has become increasingly frustrated with ⁠Serbia’s lack of ​reforms over the judiciary, rule of law and corruption. In a report this month after a ​visit to Serbia, a delegation from rights body the Council of Europe noted the “hostile and aggressive rhetoric” against opponents. And in September, E.U. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the huge public funeral of convicted ​war criminal Ratko Mladic held in Belgrade, saying it contradicted “the values underpinning Serbia’s path towards the European Union.”

articles.title: Israeli elections: What are the possible outcomes?
articles.summary: Israelis face a pivotal election on October 27, as Netanyahu’s leadership hangs in the balance amid coalition debates.
articles.body:
Israel is heading to the polls on October 27 in an election that could end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s long grip on power.

The vote for all 120 seats in the Knesset is the first since the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023, the onset of Israel’s subsequent genocidal war on Gaza and a wider conflict that has seen Israel carry out attacks in several countries across the region.

Opinion polls suggest his right-wing bloc is in a close race against a Jewish-led opposition alliance. But defeating Netanyahu at the ballot box does not necessarily mean removing him from power.

Israel’s proportional representation system means parties must negotiate alliances to secure a governing majority in the Knesset. No single party has ever won an outright majority of at least 61 seats.

According to recent polling, the opposition bloc is projected to win 52 seats, compared with 50 for Netanyahu’s religious-nationalist alliance. Palestinian-led parties could, therefore, determine who governs.

Despite slightly trailing in opinion polls, Netanyahu could remain prime minister if his Likud party assembles enough parliamentary support from existing allies or new coalition partners.

His traditional partners include far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power party and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism party.

Ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and United Torah Judaism – which have previously joined his coalition multiple times but also walked away, most recently in 2025 – could also play an important role.

In late September, four opposition parties signed a non-aggression pact, agreeing to work together in a bid to unseat Netanyahu.

The rival movements – the Yashar party, the Democrats, the Yisrael Beytenu party and the Together alliance – said they are united in their goal to “preserve and strengthen Israel as a Jewish and democratic state”.

The bloc has not announced who would lead a future governing coalition, but former army chief Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, is seen as its most likely prime ministerial candidate.

Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, who heads the Together alliance with Yair Lapid, is another potential candidate.

The Joint List and Ra’am – the two Arab-led parties representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 20 percent of the population – are projected to win about 13 seats.

Ra’am, also known as the United Arab List, made history in 2021 by joining Bennett’s coalition, becoming the first Arab-led party to participate in an Israeli governing coalition.

Mansour Abbas , leader of Ra’am, has signalled a willingness to repeat that arrangement if the opposition-led alliance needs additional seats.

He has said his priorities include combatting the wave of violent crime that has been allowed to engulf Palestinian communities, as well as addressing discriminatory government policies, including on housing.

However, most opposition leaders, including Eisenkot, have ruled out such an alliance.

If a coalition falls short of 61 seats, it could seek outside parliamentary support from other parties without including them in government, such as the Palestinian-led parties.

Joint List, which includes the Hadash, Ta’al and Balad factions, has said it could provide a so-called safety net to the anti-Netanyahu coalition by agreeing not to stand against it in a confidence vote, even if the alliance does not join the government. In return, it has said it would demand certain conditions, including a path to Palestinian statehood and fighting organised crime.

However, any such arrangement would leave the governing coalition vulnerable to defections and disputes over major policies.

A national unity government, according to Israel’s parliament, is a “government based on a broad coalition, the members of which also include representatives of rival parliamentary groups”.

This is usually formed at times of national emergencies, such as war, natural disasters or economic crises.

In May 2020, Netanyahu and Benny Gantz formed a unity government following three inconclusive elections. That agreement collapsed within a year.

However, in 2023, following the Hamas-led attacks on Israel, Gantz and members of his party joined Netanyahu’s coalition – seen as an emergency unity government – despite Gantz previously bitterly opposing it.

Two political leaders could agree to alternate as prime minister under a power-sharing arrangement.

Netanyahu and Gantz agreed to such a rotation in 2020, but their coalition collapsed before Gantz could take over.

Bennett and Lapid made the same arrangement for the prime minister’s office to change hands after the former came into power in June 2021. After Bennett’s coalition lost its parliamentary majority in June 2022, Lapid took over as caretaker prime minister in July that year.

A different prime minister from the same political camp

In Israel, the prime minister is voted in by members of the Knesset after an election.

If negotiations stall over forming a government, parties could agree to support another Knesset member from Netanyahu’s political camp or that of an opposition bloc, someone who is more acceptable to future partners.

If no leader can assemble sufficient support in the Knesset, Israel could face another period of political turbulence and head for a new election.

The country held five elections between 2019 and 2022 as rival blocs repeatedly struggled to form stable governments.

In such a scenario, Netanyahu would remain caretaker prime minister until a new administration took office.

articles.title: Teesdale residents say heating oil price 'more than double' last year
articles.summary: Middleton in Teesdale has no mains gas supply so many residents use expensive heating oil.
articles.body:
Households in Upper Teesdale are preparing for winter with the cost of heating oil "more than double" what it was compared to this time last year.

With no mains gas supply in Middleton-in-Teesdale, most homes in the area rely on heating oil to keep warm, meaning residents can face bills of more than £1,000 at a time to fill their tanks.

Recent figures suggest households across rural areas including Teesdale, Weardale, Northumberland and parts of North Yorkshire are currently paying around £600 for a 500-litre delivery of heating oil, equivalent to about £1.19 per litre.

In October 2025, domestic heating oil prices were around 52p per litre.

The rise is creating concern in communities where many residents have little choice but to rely on oil-fired heating systems.

Upper Teesdale Agricultural Support Services (UTASS), based in Middleton-in-Teesdale, run a heating oil buying group aimed at helping residents secure lower prices.

By combining orders from households across the area and placing monthly bulk purchases, the scheme can reduce costs by around 3p per litre.

The organisation says the group has become an important way of helping people manage household budgets during periods of high energy costs.

Emma Spry, the manager at UTASS, says the scheme helps with residents' "cash flow".

"To get a discount on oil you need to be buying more than 1000 litres at a time, with our scheme the minimum order is 500 litres so this can help to spread the cost a bit for people," Spry said.

UTASS itself relies on heating oil to warm its offices.

Kim Richardson, who has lived in Middleton in Teesdale for more than 20 years, said "the price of oil has shot up, it's double what it was last year".

"I need 1,000 litres, it'll be a fortune.

"My husband turns the heating off but I like it on, I like to be warm.

"Thankfully, the good summer we had meant we didn't need to use much oil during the summer months."

Many households in the area try to plan ahead by filling tanks during the warmer months when prices can sometimes be lower.

For some, however, the cost of heating oil is entirely unaffordable.

Pauline Thompson, who lives locally, says she does not use heating oil due to the cost, instead she uses oil filled radiators that use electricity to heat up.

"If we need hot water for a bath, I boil the kettle. Heating oil is just too expensive to use.

"When I moved in, I rang the electricity board and asked for the cheapest way to heat the house and they said oil radiators which use electricity to heat up so I use them instead, I'm on pension credits, it's just not affordable for me."

Without access to mains gas, residents have fewer options when heating costs increase.

As winter draws closer, organisations such as UTASS are encouraging anyone concerned about heating oil costs to explore schemes that could help reduce the price they pay.

articles.title: Wellbeing support demand for cancer patients in Jersey grows
articles.summary: Macmillan Cancer Support Jersey publishes its annual report looking back at 2025.
articles.body:
A cancer charity has seen an increase in demand for wellbeing support over the past five years, a reports says.

Macmillan Cancer Support Jersey published its annual report which looked back at the charity's work during 2025 and the progress made over its five year strategy period from 2021 to 2025.

The charity said counselling and higher-level emotional-support sessions more than doubled in Jersey from 407 in 2021 to 835 in 2025 - an increase of 105%.

Steph Gibaut, chief executive officer of Macmillan Jersey, said: "Behind every figure in this report is a person, a family and a moment when support mattered".

She added: "Over the past five years, we have transformed the way we support people affected by cancer.

"We are identifying needs earlier, offering more personalised care and providing a wider range of emotional, practical and wellbeing support."

The report found complementary therapy sessions rose from 405 in 2021 to a record 965 in 2025, representing an increase of 138%.

It also found the charity delivered 4,253 support sessions to Islanders affected by cancer in 2025.

Additionally, 308 people accessed its drop-in cancer support and wellbeing centre without a referral.

The charity said over its five-year strategy period it generated £4.38m in income and invested £3.44m in delivering and developing services for Islanders affected by cancer.

Macmillan Cancer Support Jersey said a major development was the introduction of holistic needs assessments which was formally launched after a pilot.

It said these helped identify a person's "physical, emotional, practical and financial needs earlier in their cancer experience, allowing an individual care plan to be put in place"

The report also showed the charity raised £963,090 in 2025 and invested £890,352 in its work.

The charity said fundraising highlights included the Tour des Pyrénées, which saw 52 cyclists complete a coast-to-coast challenge and raise a "record-breaking" £236,000 for the charity.

Gibaut said: "We are incredibly proud of what has been achieved, but we also know that demand continues to grow and people's needs are changing."

It said the new 2026 to 2030 strategy would focus on expanding emotional, wellbeing and group support and expanding services for people living with and beyond cancer.

articles.title: The Stroud woman whose short story inspired Hollywood film Wicker
articles.summary: Author Ursula Wills says the story was inspired by a camping trip in Cornwall 20 years ago.
articles.body:
An author who was inspired to write a short story after seeing wicker sculptures on a camping trip has said she never imagined it would become a raunchy A-list feature film.

Ursula Wills from Stroud, in Gloucestershire, had just returned from a holiday in Cornwall in 2006 when she wrote The Wicker Husband, which follows an ostracised fisherwoman who pays a basket-maker to weave her a husband.

The story was picked up by writers who "livened it up" for the big screen to become Wicker, starring Olivia Colman, Alexander Skarsgård and Peter Dinklage.

Wills called it a "unique and amazing" film that she thinks "audiences are going to go crazy for".

'They knew she was ill - days later she killed her three kids'

The 'most haunted' pubs and hotels where guests cannot explain encounters

The author, who completed a Master of Arts degree at Bath Spa University in 2004, and spent 19 years living in Bristol, drew inspiration for the 14-page story on a camping trip.

"I'd visited this place called Melinsey Mill, which is an old watermill, where a basket maker had created an art trail around the pond, with big wicker sculptures like a stag, a giant spider, and a wicker man fishing, and I thought what would anyone want a wicker man for?" she said.

"I had the idea for the story straight away."

Wills posted The Wicker Husband on a short story website called East of the Web.

After racking up interest from readers, she was contacted by actor Rhys Jennings who, alongside Olivier Award–winning composer Darren Clark, created a musical.

In March 2020, it opened at Watermill Theatre in Newbury, but after only four nights the theatre had to close because of the Covid-19 pandemic.

A year later, she was approached by producer Justin Lothrop who asked her for film rights.

"I had a meeting with writers and directors, but after Olivia Colman came onboard in 2023 things rolled out really fast," Wills said.

"By the end of 2024 I was out in Budapest where the film was being shot.

"When I read the script, I thought it was going to be good, and when I saw it being shot in Hungary I knew it - the end result is something unique and amazing.

"I think audiences are going to go crazy for it."

Wicker, which opens in UK cinemas on 30 October and has been described as a raunchy fantasy rom-com, has garnered lots of attention online and spawned countless viral posts .

Although Wills has said the finished film remains faithful to her original short story, the intimate relationship between the fisherwoman and her wicker husband has been embellished to "liven it up".

Joint writer-directors Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson said they "loved it immediately".

"It was very sort of sparsely written, but just had these beautiful little clues throughout that suggested to us what the tone of the film could become," they explained.

"We realised this was more than a period fable. We immediately saw a satirical comedy about sex and marriage, a unique visual spectacle, and a strange love story that would ground it all."

The UK premiere for the film was held earlier this month at the British Film Institute in London.

"I had to scuttle away from the afterparty at 21:45 to get the train back to Swindon and then I had to get a rail replacement bus to Stroud," she said.

Wills now has a literary agent, and has a new collection of 13 short stories coming out across the world in April.

However, she explained the journey of The Wicker Husband was not over yet.

"I wouldn't have predicted that it was going to be a full film with an A-list cast, but I did think that it would find a home somewhere," she said.

"It's got legs and it's not finished walking yet".

articles.title: Seabirds and sewage among Isle of Man Biosphere status challenges
articles.summary: A report marking 10 years of the Isle of Man as a UNESCO Biosphere highlights the scheme's progress.
articles.body:
Sewage being discharged into the sea and under-threat seabirds are among the challenges facing the Isle of Man after a decade as a UNESCO Biosphere, a report has said.

The State of the Biosphere report looks back on the 10 years since the island became the world's first whole-nation Biosphere in 2016, in recognition of its thriving natural habitats from returning wildlife to new marine reserves.

But it warns that while some wildlife is recovering, many species and habitats are still in long-term decline.

It comes ahead of a UNESCO decision next summer on whether the island will keep its status.

UNESCO (the United Nations' agency for education, science and culture) Biosphere status recognises places that balance protecting nature with supporting people, communities and the economy.

The Isle of Man became the first entire country, including its surrounding seas, to be given the status, which is reviewed every 10 years.

Among the successes of the Biosphere's first decade was the return of juniper, a native shrub that had been lost from the island.

The last native plant on the island was dug up from Glen Auldyn in 1947 in an attempt to save it, but died soon afterwards.

Since 2016, it has been replanted in the uplands, with surveys showing "encouraging survival and growth".

Meanwhile on the Calf of Man, controlling rats - referred to locally as "longtails" to avoid bad luck - has helped the Manx shearwater recover to about 1,500 breeding pairs.

Nine new Marine Nature Reserves have been created since 2016, and together they now cover more than half the sea within three nautical miles of the coast.

By the end of last year, 420 hectares of damaged peatland had also been restored.

A 2024 assessment found 48 of the 166 bird species regularly seen on the island were on the red list of greatest conservation concern. Another cause for concern was that monitoring has found declines in young salmon.

The report also acknowledges sewage is still being discharged into the sea at Peel and in Garff, though work on a new treatment works for Peel began last year.

It says Biosphere status is "not a claim that everything is working as it should", and that its credibility depends partly on being prepared to admit where it is not.

Biosphere Isle of Man chairman Jason Bissell said there was "much to celebrate from our first decade, and much still to do".

The report has been published alongside an exhibition at the Manx Museum entitled Jeihosphere, which tells the Biosphere's story through 10 objects, running until 28 February.

articles.title: Kochi man, 55, killed as Mercedes driven by judge’s minor son hits scooter
articles.summary: KOCHI: A Mercedes-Benz driven by a minor rammed into a scooter in Kochi early Sunday, killing a 55-year-old man.
articles.body: KOCHI: A Mercedes-Benz driven by a minor rammed into a scooter in Kochi early Sunday, killing a 55-year-old man. Police sources said the child in conflict with the law was the son of a judge.The deceased was identified as Jayabalakrishnan (55), son of Rangaswamy Chettiyar, a resident of South Chittoor.He ran a roadside eatery and was heading home after closing the shop when the accident occurred around 2.20 am on Container Road near Maraparamb in Cheranelloor.Both vehicles were travelling in the same direction towards Kalamassery. A preliminary investigation indicated that the car hit the scooter from behind, police said.An FIR has been registered under Sections 281 and 106(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita for rash driving and causing death by negligence. A senior officer with Cheranelloor police said the minor’s medical examination report had been received.The doctor’s preliminary report indicated that he had not consumed alcohol, but a detailed report would be sought.The officer added that the sections would be altered if the investigation revealed any further offence. The preliminary investigation indicated that the minor was alone in the car.Although the offences under the sections invoked are bailable, police said further action would be taken after consulting the Juvenile Justice Board.Meanwhile, Jayalakshmi, a relative of the victim, said she visited the accident spot and found the scene horrifying.“One of his footwear items was on the road, while the other chappal and helmet were at a distance on the service road. The impact on the vehicles itself showed that it was a high-intensity collision,” she told reporters.Police have not disclosed the accused’s identity, as Section 74 of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act prohibits the disclosure of a child in conflict with the law’s identity or any particulars that could lead to identification.According to police, the teenager claimed in his initial statement that the scooter suddenly swerved to avoid waterlogging and that he could not stop in time to avoid the collision. Heavy rain had also lashed the area in the early hours of Sunday.The accident comes close on the heels of another high-profile crash in Kochi on October 11, when a Mini Cooper driven by a 19-year-old rammed into a scooter, killing three youths.Suhail (19), who was behind the wheel of the luxury hatchback, was allegedly intoxicated and driving at an extremely high speed. articles.title: Open mic event in Bournemouth giving artists a voice
articles.summary: Jack and Yannick have run the events as OPB Collective since 2024, and have helped platform a variety of creatives
articles.body:
At 21 years old Jack Townsend is already doing it all - rapping, writing, producing and running a project designed to help connect young artists - alongside best friend Yannick Manhica.

Under the OPB Studios name, the pair host an open-mic night in Bournemouth, which is running all month after its relaunch at the Helch Market venue.

The events helps connect talent in the area and have introduced a space where people "feel they can belong," says Yannick.

The pair's events attract creatives including singers, poets, dancers, designers and DJs from across Hampshire and Dorset.

Yannick, 26, got the idea for OPB, which stands for orange, pink and blue as well as opulence, passion and bravery, six years ago on his 20th birthday.

"Over the years, I've collected a lot of people that are very talented artists," he says.

"I started getting loads of people come to me directly and be like, 'I know you know lots of people, can you help me out with something?' And I was like 'oh cool - this is dope'."

After meeting Jack, he says everything changed and the pair decided to launch their first open mic together in December 2024.

They took a break from the business but in the summer of 2025 they held an the event in Bournemouth Square for 17 weeks.

This October have come back to where they started, hosting nights in the underground speakeasy bar.

Anyone is welcome - acts include singers, rappers, DJs, poets, and comedians.

Yannick says they never quite know what they are going to get on any given night and that artists just "appreciate the space" they have created.

Bartender Andre, who produces hybrid melodic-metal, hip-hop and country western music, says: "It feels like Bournemouth is coming on its way back up again.

"Music is the one thing that can bring people together. It puts things into perspective - maybe things aren't as bad as they seem."

"It's not clique-y here," says Madeleine, who premiered her original song Daddy's Attitude at the event on Wednesday.

Her and her friends, Helena Yasmin, 25, and Jenny, 26, who also write and perform their own music, moved back to Bournemouth after university.

Madeleine says they are "falling back in love" with their hometown and that they feel things may be changing for the better through the arts.

"As a teenager, I fully rejected the town," she says.

"Then coming back as an adult, it was like, 'wait, there's loads of things to do'.

"And with things like this, it's something where I can bring all my friends. It is really good vibes."

articles.title: Storm Boelo: Flight disruption and thousands without electricity
articles.summary: Flights have been cancelled in Belfast and Dublin, while thousands of homes have been left without power.
articles.body:
Thousands of homes across the island of Ireland are without power after Storm Boelo.

Northern Ireland Electricity (NIE) said 7,000 customers have been affected, while about 41,000 homes, farms and businesses across the Republic of Ireland are without electricity on Sunday morning.

The worst impacted areas in Northern Ireland include Springfield in County Fermanagh and Bushmills in County Antrim, where more than 1,000 homes near each village are without power.

Flights have also been cancelled at Belfast City, Belfast International and Dublin Airports due to the storm.

An NIE spokesperson said high winds and severe weather conditions during Saturday night and into the early hours of Sunday morning resulted in a "level of damage to the electricity network, leading to power outages for some customers".

NIE said customers can check estimated restoration times using its Powercheck tool .

A spokesperson for the Republic of Ireland's ESB Networks said properties in the north west of the country are primarily affected.

"As Met Éireann weather warnings remain in place, there may be further power outages this morning," they said.

Among the villages worst affected in the Republic of Ireland is Milford in County Donegal with more 1,600 homes without power and Aghagad in County Sligo with over 1,200 homes impacted.

ESB Networks said crews have been deployed to all impacted areas and they "expect the vast majority of impacted customers to have their supply restored by this evening".

A yellow weather warning for all of Northern Ireland is in place until midday while a yellow wind warning is also in place in County Donegal until 15:00 local time on Sunday.

Storm Boelo brings 85mph gusts and travel disruption with amber weather warnings in effect

Flights cancelled at Belfast and Dublin airports

At Belfast City Airport, flights departing to Edinburgh, Cardiff, Manchester and Kirkwall on Sunday morning have been cancelled.

Meanwhile, flights arriving from Edinburgh, Leeds Bradford, Cardiff, Manchester, Birmingham and Inverness have also been cancelled.

At Belfast International Airport, 17 flights have been cancelled this morning.

"Storm Boelo continues to cause some disruption to flights today. Please check with your airline for latest flight information as delays can be expected," a spokesperson said.

At Dublin Airport, strong winds continue to have an impact on flight operations on Sunday.

"Mainly due to weather issues in other countries, airlines have so far cancelled 12 inbound and 12 outbound flights," Graeme McQueen from the airport's operator daa has said.

He advised passengers to travel to the airport as normal and keep in contact with their airline, adding that further disruption is possible due to the wind warnings.

The Stena Line ferry sailings from Belfast to Cairnryan and Liverpool on Sunday morning have been cancelled.

Stena Line sailings from Cairnryan to Belfast have also been impacted.

The Stena Line sailing between Dublin and Holyhead has not been affected.

Sailings with P&O Ferries from Cairnryan and Larne at 08:00 and 12:00 on Sunday have also been cancelled due to the storm.

A number of roads across Northern Ireland have been closed due to fallen trees, the police have said.

The Springwell Road in Groomsport, County Down, is closed due to a fallen tree, while the Cootehall Road, Crawfordsburn, has been reduced to one lane due to another fallen tree.

The Ballyrobin Road in County Antrim and the Glenshane Road in County Londonderry have reopened after they were impassible earlier on Sunday morning.

An amber warning across parts of County Antrim and County Londonderry ended at 10:00 GMT on Sunday.

On Saturday, Northern Ireland's strongest gust of wind reached 78mph and was recorded in Orlock Head, County Down.

Magilligan in County Londonderry recorded 73mph and Castlederg in County Tyrone recorded a wind gust of 70mph.

Westerly winds will continue to gust close to 70mph in exposed coastal areas until well into the afternoon.

Generally, though winds will gradually ease through the afternoon with a significant reduction this evening.

An orange wind warning ended in County Donegal at 09:00 local time on Sunday.

On Saturday, Malin Head in Donegal had gusts of 83mph recorded.

The last 24 hours also brought notable amounts of rain with Castlederg and Lough Fea in the Sperrins recording almost 40mm.

Over 30mm has been recorded at Killylane in the Antrim Glens and 30mm at Stormont in Belfast.

Sunday is due to be a drier day but still very windy with some sunshine and occasional passing showers.

The disturbed weather pattern will continue into the half term week as another deep area of low pressure will bring more strong winds later on Monday and through to Tuesday.

The Met Office has issued a yellow wind warning across parts of Northern Ireland for this system which may be updated later on Sunday.

The second half of the new week, however, looks somewhat quieter, drier, and less windy.

articles.title: Why is Egypt so wary of getting involved in Yemen’s conflict?
articles.summary: As Egypt considers defending Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks, memories of its war in Yemen in the 1960s loom large.
articles.body:
Egyptian forces arrived in Yemen in the thousands, backing the country’s government in a civil war against rebels that threatened to overthrow it.

But this is not today’s war – this is 1962, and the Egyptians were supporting republican forces in North Yemen against the country’s royalists. The intervention came after Yemenis who were friendlier to the Arab nationalist ideology propagated by Egypt under President Gamal Abdel Nasser led a revolution that overthrew Zaidi Imam Mohammad al-Badr – a theocratic monarch.

Although the republican side was ultimately successful in the war against the Saudi-backed royalists, Egyptian forces withdrew in the wake of their defeat in the 1967 war against Israel , and after also suffering heavy losses in Yemen.

Suggestions of a new military intervention by Egypt in Yemen today, after comments by President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, are therefore bringing back memories of that period for Egyptians.

Following some backlash against the suggestion of direct military intervention, el-Sisi emphasised on Wednesday that any military deployment would be focused on defending Saudi Arabia, and would not involve any direct aggression against Yemen’s Houthi rebels.

And on Thursday, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty called for a political solution to the conflict.

What has the Egyptian government said it will do?

After Saudi Arabia came under more intense attacks from the Houthis, including a strike on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh which killed 13 people, including one Egyptian, earlier this month, it appears that the kingdom expects support from its longtime allies, including Egypt.

Some countries, including Turkiye, Pakistan, France and the United Kingdom , have already deployed forces to Saudi Arabia in defensive operations or have indicated they are willing to do so.

Saudi Arabia has faced repeated Houthi ballistic missile and drone attacks as the war in Yemen escalated over the past few months, particularly after a Saudi-backed Yemeni government counteroffensive against the Houthis began in early October. Saudi Arabia has supported a counteroffensive by forces allied to the internationally recognised government, with air raids against the Houthis.

Egypt’s National Defence Council said on October 18 the country was ready to provide “all necessary and possible support to Saudi Arabia to defend its safety and stability”.

While much has been made of the possibility of an Egyptian deployment, Cairo has repeatedly made it clear that it has no intention of involving itself in direct attacks against the Houthis.

But even a defensive combat mission would involve the deployment of Egyptian forces outside the country’s borders, so it requires approval from the Egyptian parliament. A vote is scheduled for Monday, after a weeklong delay to allow reticent lawmakers to deliberate on this move.

Why is Egypt wary of becoming involved in Yemen?

This apprehension over military involvement in Yemen is largely related to the Egyptian government’s desire to avoid foreign military entanglements and direct involvement in the US-Israel war on Iran and its allies.

Active participation in attacks against the Houthis could open Egypt up to retaliation by the group or Iran. The Houthis have already shown they are capable of pinpoint attacks on vital civilian and military targets in Saudi Arabia.

An expansion of Houthi attacks on Red Sea shipping – both Egyptian and otherwise – would also be highly damaging to Egypt’s economy, as the country controls its northern entry point, the Suez Canal, and is heavily reliant on this waterway for trade.

Fewer ships passing through the Red Sea means fewer fees paid to the Egyptian government for their passage through the Suez Canal. El-Sisi has said Egypt has already lost $20bn in potential revenues over the last few years due to regional instability, including previous attacks on ships in the Red Sea and the turmoil in the Strait of Hormuz caused by the US-Israel war on Iran.

Disruptions to energy supplies via the Bab al-Mandeb now, which the Houthis effectively control, would likely lead to higher oil prices and knock-on effects for net consumers such as Egypt.

There is also the historical aspect. While Egypt can argue that its intervention in Yemen in the 1960s was an overall success, with the Republican side eventually emerging victorious, the campaign in mountainous northwestern Yemen was brutal. Thousands of Egyptian soldiers were killed in the campaign, and this was blamed by some for the Egyptian military’s lack of readiness in confronting Israel in the 1967 war.

“There is the memory that [Egypt] went to Yemen and faced forces supported by Saudi Arabia, and Egyptian troops were killed there,” said Ahmad Dahshan, the editor-in-chief of the Center of Arabic Eurasian Studies. “Then [the mentality is] that Egypt will send troops to Yemen once again, where they would also be killed, but this time on behalf of Saudi Arabia.”

While Egypt has not detailed what “defensive” military assistance it could provide, judging by the support supplied by other countries aiding Saudi Arabia, this could include operating air defence equipment and interceptors to protect the kingdom from missiles and drones or guarding sensitive sites.

Even this could lead to the deaths of foreign soldiers, as Houthi strikes have so far targeted sites in Saudi Arabia they perceive to be strategically important, including those that Egyptian personnel could be deployed to.

There is also potential for naval assistance in the Red Sea to protect shipping, and forces stationed on the Saudi-Yemeni border to reinforce security there, which have also been targets.

“These troops would only be deployed, if they are deployed at all, to contribute to the protection of Saudi territory,” Dahshan said. “The discussion this time may be taking place because there is a possibility of ground troops being deployed to protect the Saudi border against any attempted Houthi incursion.”

How important is foreign support for Yemen?

Egypt was officially part of the Saudi-led coalition to restore the Yemeni government in 2015, but played only a limited role in operations. However, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have played decisive roles during the war, with other countries such as Sudan at times contributing fighters on the ground.

Saudi Arabia and the UAE not only conducted heavy bombing campaigns against the Houthis, but also had forces in the country coordinating with the Yemeni military and anti-Houthi groups. This exposed both countries to Houthi attacks.

But some Yemenis on the anti-Houthi side blame foreign forces, in particular the UAE, for undermining the independence of the Yemeni government. The UAE was allegedly a major supporter of the Southern Transitional Council, and was eventually forced out of Yemen at the start of the year following a Saudi-backed Yemeni government push to defeat southern secessionists.

While Saudi air support has been a huge advantage for Yemeni government forces over the Houthis, many observers say that the pro-government side does not need additional manpower on the ground.

“The Yemeni government just needs political support and economic support, and that has been the case since the war started,” said Mohammed al-Qadhi, an independent Yemeni political and conflict analyst. “The Yemeni government has enough fighters … it lacks weapons and economic support, as well as logistical and technical support. It needs better coordination and command and control for the forces on the ground.”

As for the prospect of any Egyptian involvement, al-Qadhi said many Yemenis remain indebted to Egypt for the support it has provided the republic in the past.

“Yemenis still cherish the Egyptian role with pride and respect … Without the Egyptian role and Nasser’s support, the republic would not have existed,” al-Qadhi said. “The Houthis recall history and how the Egyptian support in defending the republic was vital … though I dismiss a similar role for the Egyptian army today.”

articles.title: Brazil votes in pivotal runoff between Lula and Bolsonaro Jr.
articles.summary: SAO PAULO — Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday in a tight runoff vote that could shift ⁠Latin America’s largest nation sharply rightward, bringing it closer to the United States as part of a broader conservative shift across the region.
articles.body: SAO PAULO — Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday in a tight runoff vote that could shift ⁠Latin America’s largest nation sharply rightward, bringing it closer to the United States as part of a broader conservative shift across the region. The runoff pits leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio scored a major upset at the start of the ⁠month by defying pollsters to lead voting in the ​first ⁠round. A victory for Bolsonaro, 45, would extend a wave of right-wing victories for Latin American candidates friendly to US President Donald Trump, while a fourth mandate for Lula ⁠would be a disappointment in Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security. The ​election ⁠race has been dominated by corruption ‌scandals, economic anxiety and accusations of U.S. meddling, which Washington denies. It has also been colored by fallout from Jair Bolsonaro’s 2025 conviction for plotting a 2022 coup, with Flavio pledging to free ‌his father if he is elected. Trump has called the ‌case a “witch hunt” and imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil in 2025, in a decision explicitly linked to Jair Bolsonaro’s trial. While many of those were later watered down, Trump unleashed new levies against Brazil this year, citing unfair trade practices. Lula ⁠has cast the Trump administration’s proximity to the Bolsonaro clan as part of an attempt to sway the election, while labeling tariffs and other punitive measures as bullying. On economic issues, despite falling inequality and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over an electorate grappling with high living costs and heavy household debt. Endemic gang violence also weighs on voters’ minds. Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living concerns and has also promised a heavy-handed approach to fighting crime, pledging maximum-security jails ‌and chemical castration for serious sexual offenses. Candidates are neck and neck Polls show the candidates ​are practically tied going into the runoff, as Lula has closed the gap ‌in the final days. Historical precedent favors Bolsonaro, ⁠however, as no candidate has ever won the presidency after coming second in the first-round ⁠vote. Bolsonaro picked up 47% of ballots cast in the first round, while Lula trailed with 45%. The senator’s first-round win ‌sent Brazil’s markets and currency soaring ​on expectations of pro-business reforms. His first-round success ‌was mirrored in congressional elections for his Liberal ​Party and other right-wing politicians, which could pave a legislative path for him, or complicate governance for Lula.

articles.title: That Girl Boina: How employee theft is hurting small businesses in Africa
articles.summary: That Girl Boina's post about why she had closed her beauty parlour struck a nerve with other small business owners.
articles.body:
When popular Kenyan food creator That Girl Boina took a two-week holiday to Europe, she expected to relax. A week into the trip, an Instagram direct message exposed a problem that would ultimately lead to the closure of her business.

"I was at your studio, I liked everything. The only problem was that I was asked to send money to a different number. It wasn't the number on the wall," a customer wrote to her.

Boina had opened Waxaholic Studio, a waxing and hydrafacial parlour in Nairobi's central business district, on 1 September 2024. A year later, she had hired a receptionist and two specialists and felt confident enough to take a two-week holiday, her first international trip of the year.

"I trusted them. It's two rooms and a reception - how do you mess that up?" she recalls thinking.

"It never occurred to me that maybe I was getting clients and someone else was stealing from me," she tells the BBC.

The discovery prompted Boina to examine the business more closely. Although the business had made a profit in the first few months, revenue began to fall in early 2025. She initially dismissed the decline as a seasonal slump but then realised there was a problem.

"Everyone around was making money apart from me," she says in hindsight.

She had already considered closing because it was not making a profit, but her initial investment, three employees depending on the business and her vision for it kept her going. The customer's message became the turning-point.

"If I am not making money and I am willing to wait and see where this goes and you guys are not giving me the same energy, then why are we still open?"

Rather than confront the employees, Boina decided to close the studio. That weekend, she put it up for sale but found no buyer. She sold some of the equipment and took others, including decorations, home. Waxaholic Studio closed in October 2025.

"I remember my friend taking me to a restaurant, and I started crying. We were both silent."

Boina describes the experience as the worst feeling she has ever felt. The closure was not just a financial setback, but the loss of something she had built to secure her future.

In September, nearly a year after the business closed, Boina shared a video on TikTok recounting the experience, explaining that she had needed time to heal before speaking publicly about what happened.

The video went viral after being reposted on X, formerly Twitter, garnering close to one million views. It drew responses from many Kenyan business owners who described how theft, ranging from payment diversion to stock theft and the sale of expensive equipment, had pushed their businesses to the brink, forcing them to fire staff, sell their businesses or shut down.

"Although I have recovered emotionally, I am yet to recoup the money I invested in setting up and running the studio," says Boina.

The reaction to her story showed that employee theft is a huge problem for many small businesses owners in Africa, where a handful of employees may control payments, stock and supplier transactions, often with limited oversight.

A 2022 survey by PwC, one of the world's biggest consultancy firms, found that 63% of respondents in East Africa said their organisations had experienced economic crime, compared to a global figure of 46%.

The risks are not confined to small businesses. Some of East Africa's biggest supermarkets have also reported significant losses linked to employee fraud and stock theft. Tuskys and Nakumatt have both collapsed this decade amid wider financial and operational problems partly attributed to employee theft.

At its peak, Tuskys had more than 6,000 employees and over 60 branches across Kenya and Uganda. In 2015, the retailer hired loss-prevention firm Hipora Business Solutions East Africa to help tackle fraud. An audit found that Tuskys was losing more than 100m Kenya shillings (£581,000; $770,000) a month to employee theft, Business Daily reported. The alleged schemes included cashiers pocketing money, manipulating till transactions, and colluding with suppliers over goods received.

Nakumatt also suffered significant stock losses attributed to employee theft before going under, with a Kenyan policy firm reporting that more than $100m (£75m) worth of stock was unaccounted for.

Hipora, which works with businesses across East and Southern Africa, says employee theft is a huge problem, estimating that it accounts for more than 60% of losses recorded by small businesses.

Employee theft has evolved over the years, Hipora boss John Wanjohi tells the BBC. "Employees are like a cartel that colludes with clients and suppliers to perpetuate theft."

Employee theft does not always involve money being diverted to an employee's phone. It can sometimes take subtle forms, making it harder for business owners to detect.

For Cris Njoki, founder of IKOJN, a Kenyan ready-to-wear clothes brand, the problem lay further up the supply chain.

"I found out that one of my staff was asking our suppliers to quote higher for some of the raw materials we were getting from them," she says.

The employee allegedly colluded with a supplier to inflate prices, with the two sharing the excess money after the company paid the invoices. Njoki investigated the scheme and confronted the employee with the evidence. The employee subsequently left the company.

Since then, Njoki has tightened her firm's procurement controls.

"We have now centralised the procurement process and created a paper trail. Finance speaks to the supplier and then makes payment," she tells the BBC.

Across the continent in Accra, Ghana, employee theft came close to bringing Muftawu Nabila's business to an end.

The Joy News sports journalist says he was robbed by two different employees in the four years he has run his electronics shop. But theft by a third employee, he says, nearly forced him to close it altogether.

His first employee was let off with a warning. The second tripled monthly sales but left when her university semester resumed.

Before traveling to the United States to cover the Fifa World Cup in June 2026, Nabila hired a third attendant, leaving the business with little supervision.

"She almost collapsed my shop," he says.

While other employees had taken smaller amounts, sometimes as little as 50 cedis ($4; £3) at a time, the third attendant was operating on a larger scale, he says.

"Assuming we are making a sale of $200 (£150) a day, she could take up to $30," he says.

The theft continued for two months. When Nabila tried to restock the shop, he realised the money coming in was not enough to replenish his shelves. He began counting his stock every morning.

When he confronted the employee, she denied the allegations. But a stock count she conducted herself revealed a significant gap between inventory and sales receipts.

"I just told her: 'If you go home today, don't come back,'" he says.

His salary from his journalism job allowed him to rebuild the business.

For him, the shop is a way of creating jobs, making the theft particularly frustrating.

"We have to generate the money from the shop for me to pay you. So if I pay you, pay electricity bills, shop rent and you steal some, where am I expected to generate money?"

Theft happens in businesses around the world, but its consequences can be particularly severe for small businesses in Africa.

Many operate on tight margins, with limited access to finance, high borrowing costs and unpredictable tax environments.

Purchasing power is also lower in many African markets, limiting how much businesses can recover through sales or pass on to customers.

This is especially significant in a continent where the informal economy accounts for a large share of employment and economic activity.

For businesses without much of a financial cushion, the loss of cash, stock or equipment can threaten their ability to pay staff, restock or keep operating.

What might be a manageable loss for a larger company can push a small business to the wall.

Wanjohi says many small businesses lack proper safeguards to prevent theft.

At one struggling pharmacy branch, his team tightened controls over cash handling, stock movements, and cashier operations. Wanjohi says daily sales subsequently increased from 80,000 Kenya shillings to 200,000 after the changes.

Wanjohi says many businesses seek help from loss-control specialists only after the problem has become serious.

Detecting suspected theft, however, is only part of the challenge. Employers must also follow the law when investigating allegations and deciding whether to dismiss an employee.

Judith Guserwa, an advocate, says employers must investigate suspected theft, gather evidence and allow employees to respond before taking disciplinary action.

If employees admit to theft and choose to repay, let it be in writing: "If they don't, you terminate with a valid reason and press charges," she says.

The experience has changed how Boina approaches hiring.

She says she will now be slow to hire and quick to fire.

"I cannot teach you integrity," she concludes.

articles.title: Obama’s Ohio, Michigan speeches: Key takeaways on Trump, Iran war, midterms
articles.summary: The former US president warns of rising costs, corruption and threats to democratic values ahead of the November 3 vote.
articles.body:
Former President Barack Obama has railed against the Trump administration on a range of issues, including dragging the United States into “an unnecessary war” against Iran, as he campaigned for Democrats in Ohio and Michigan ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

Speaking at rallies on Saturday, Obama accused President Donald Trump of “chaos and corruption”, as he urged voters to reject Republicans.

The speeches came just 10 days before the elections, with Senate and gubernatorial races taking place in both states.

Obama blames Trump’s Iran war for rising fuel prices

“The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions,” Obama said in Cleveland, Ohio, where he rallied in support of former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown.

“Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for,” Obama said.

The former president defended the 2015 nuclear agreement reached under his administration, which restricted Tehran’s nuclear programme in exchange for sanctions relief.

“Iran didn’t have nuclear weapons because I had put a deal in place that everybody acknowledged kept them from getting nukes, and I didn’t have to fire a missile to do it. I just had to engage in diplomacy,” Obama said.

Obama blamed the conflict for rising oil and diesel prices, citing attacks on US military bases, American casualties and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

“Our allies and our bases have been attacked. Americans have been killed, hundreds of Americans have been wounded. We have run down our stock of missiles, and Iran now has veto power over the Strait of Hormuz where oil goes through to the world market,” he said.

The disruptions in oil flow through the strait, located between Iran and Oman, have pushed up energy prices worldwide. Before the war, a fifth of global oil and gas passed through the strait, which Iran has used as leverage in the war.

“This is the reason why the price of oil is up … This is the reason the price of diesel is up.”

The spike in diesel and petrol prices will likely cost the Republican Party, as the majority of Americans hold Trump responsible for starting the war and the subsequent increase in prices.

Obama also mocked Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his focus on military culture and the Pentagon’s plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009.

“These are not serious people,” Obama said.

Tariffs are making life more expensive for Americans

Obama criticised Trump’s tariffs, saying Americans were paying more for goods, including products made in the US using imported parts.

“When you impose tariffs, consumers pay the tab,” he said.

“It’s not just the goods that you use directly that have been imported … It’s also the car you build here in America. They might need a part from somewhere else, and now suddenly there’s a tariff on it.”

He questioned Trump’s trade dispute with Canada, a major US trading partner.

The two countries have been locked in a trade dispute, with Trump threatening 50 percent tariffs on Canadian vehicles and auto parts from January 2027.

“And the big trade war he’s starting now is with that well-known evil empire Canada,” Obama said sarcastically.

“Canadians are the nicest people … they’re like our friendly neighbours to the north, and he’s like picking a fight with them.”

Obama also pointed to the growing US national debt, which has reached $40 trillion.

“Instead of bringing down deficits like he said with these tariffs, we’re now running a debt to the tune of $40 trillion.”

The figure refers to the total federal debt, which has accumulated over successive administrations, rather than the annual budget deficit.

Charges of corruption and enriching the wealthy

Obama accused the Trump administration of favouring wealthy Americans while common households struggled with rising costs.

“After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, ‘Enough is enough,'” Obama declared. “We are voting for change right here in Ohio.”

He pointed to Trump’s 2025 tax and spending legislation, which extended tax cuts while reducing federal spending on programmes including Medicaid and food assistance.

“The only bill they passed of any significance in the last two years was a trillion-dollar tax break that mostly benefitted the richest Americans,” he said.

Obama also took aim at Trump’s White House renovations, including plans for a ballroom, changes to the Rose Garden and the addition of gold decorations.

“He seems very focused on home renovations. He should be on HGTV,” Obama joked.

“He’s got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory, just gold everywhere.”

Obama condemns Trump’s immigration crackdown

The former president said the US needed secure borders but criticised the methods used by immigration agents under the Trump administration.

“I believe that we do need to make sure that our border is orderly and secure and that people who want to come here do so lawfully,” he said.

“But I don’t recall anybody campaigning on sending masked agents running through our streets. I don’t recall anybody talking about law-abiding citizens being arrested, detained, or shot.”

“That’s not what we have to do to get our borders under control,” he added.

In Ohio, Obama criticised Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy over a campaign advertisement featuring the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton.

The advertisement features Acton’s mother questioning her honesty and her account of her childhood, without mentioning the allegations of sexual abuse that led to their separation decades ago.

It has drawn criticism from Republicans, including Ohio Governor Mike DeWine, although Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended it.

Obama condemned Ramaswamy’s decision to use Acton’s family history in the campaign.

“There’s got to be something inside you where you just say, you know, no office is worth stooping that low,” he said.

He also praised Acton’s career in public service and urged Ohio voters to support her on November 3.

Obama urges Michigan voters to back El-Sayed and Benson

In Detroit, Obama campaigned for Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and gubernatorial contender Jocelyn Benson.

He praised El-Sayed’s Michigan roots and criticised his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, over his support for the US-Israel war on Iran and Trump’s trade policies.

“Abdul is as Michigan as it gets,” Obama said, referring to his upbringing in the state, his family’s ties to the auto industry and his involvement in school sports.

Obama also spoke about attacks on El-Sayed’s Muslim identity, comparing them with false claims about his own religion and birthplace during his presidential campaigns.

“Unlike Mike Rogers, Abdul hasn’t spent months cheerleading the Iran war … or called these tariffs ‘masterful’.”

The former president pushed back against those who call El-Sayed a “radical”, declaring that “Abdul shares my values”.

Obama also praised Benson for standing by Michigan’s 2020 election results despite threats and protests outside her home.

“When armed protesters showed up outside her home in 2020, demanded she overturn Michigan’s fair and free election results, Jocelyn stood her ground, stood up for you and your rights,” he said.

Obama calls midterms a ‘circuit breaker’ against Trump

Obama said the midterm elections offered voters a chance to limit Trump’s power during the remaining two years of his presidency.

“This election is our last best chance to at least rein in some of the foolishness of this administration,” he said. “It’s the circuit breaker in the system. We need to flip that circuit breaker.”

He also warned that dishonesty, intimidation and bullying were becoming accepted in US politics.

“We are not going to fix the economic system or the political system … so long as we’ve got a culture where anything goes and where people in the highest offices in the land think it’s OK to lie and cheat and bully,” he said.

“What we are missing in our public discourse is just basic decency.”

articles.title: Brazil 2026 election live: Lula and Bolsonaro in tight race

Incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is seeking an unprecedented fourth term in office, facing off against Senator Flavio Bolsonaro in a tightly contested presidential race , after a close first-round election on October 4.

articles.title: Storm Boelo brings flooding, power cuts and gusts of up to 84mph to Wales
articles.summary: More than 500 homes are without power and flooding and felled trees have been reported on roads.
articles.body:
Hundreds of homes were left without power on Sunday morning after back-to-back storms led to flooding and felled trees in Wales.

A wind gust of 84mph (135km/h) was recorded in Capel Curig, Conwy county, on Saturday, which also saw 2.1in (54.6mm) of rain.

Police forces and councils said they have been dealing with flooding and trees down as Storm Boelo followed Storm Austen over the weekend, while there is also significant disruption on Wales' railways.

Four flood warnings were in place in south Wales on Sunday morning, while 555 homes in Rhayader, Powys, were left without power.

About 100 homes across south Wales were also without power on Sunday morning, while SP Energy said it was dealing with 14 separate power outages in north and mid Wales.

The National Grid said its engineers were working to restore power to the households affected "as quickly as possible" and apologised for the disruption.

Most of Wales was not covered by a weather warning during Storm Boelo, although a yellow warning for wind covers parts of north Wales until 21:00 GMT on Sunday.

A total of 2.2in (55.2mm) of rain was also recorded in Bute Park in Cardiff throughout Saturday.

Buses are running instead of a number of Transport for Wales train services due to flooding and poor weather.

A TfW spokesperson said incidents included the line being blocked between Cardiff Central and Bridgend and flooding on the railway between Bridgend and Maesteg.

Rhondda Cynon Taf council said it had been dealing with numerous reports of trees down.

Natural Resources Wales had four flood warnings for the River Ely in place at 09:20.

Cowbridge Road in Ely, Cardiff, has been closed due to high water levels.

Stenaline has cancelled the 10:00 sailing from Holyhead to Dublin and said other services might be delayed because of the weather conditions.

Irish Ferries has announced it had also cancelled two sailings between Holyhead and Dublin today, adding services this afternoon might leave early.

The Pembroke to Rosslare ferry was also cancelled, with later sailings due to continue.

In north Wales, police have warned drivers of a significant amount of debris and fallen trees on the A470 between the Black Cat Roundabout and Llanrwst, Conwy county.

They urged people to "please take care when driving in this area".

Videos on social media showed cars trying drive down waterlogged roads as rain poured down drenched pavements.

Natural Resources Wales urged people hit by flooding to go to a safe place, saying: "You might have to leave your home if it is safe to do so."

On Saturday, staff at the Tafell a Tân cafe in Llangrannog, Ceredigion, praised the community for stepping in to help with a clean-up operation in the aftermath of Storm Austen.

The venue was forced to close for the day on Friday due to a sandstorm brought by Storm Austen.

Posting on social media, they said: "How lucky are we... Llangrannog at its absolute finest, thank you great people."
